note: Per-class codified methodology: deterministic steps a hunter runs by hand or wires to a tool, plus an OPTIONAL ai_hook (light AI enhancement, never required). Keyed by {family,name} resolved to the taxonomy class id at seed time. Starter set covers the top-payout classes; extend incrementally.

methodologies.name: IDOR / BOLA, iterable object identifiers, sensitive data
steps: Authenticate as account A and B. Capture a request from A that references an object id (path, query, body, header, or cookie).
Swap A's object id for B's while keeping A's session/token. Read exactly one record, never the table.
Test every id surface the UI never calls: sibling endpoints, GraphQL node(id:), export/report/print variants.
Record the delta: whose data, how many records reachable, and whether write (PUT/PATCH/DELETE) also crosses the boundary.
Stop at proof. Do not enumerate; one cross-tenant read is the finding.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to cluster captured endpoints by id-parameter shape and flag which lack an ownership check in the response diff.

methodologies.name: Broken Function Level Authorization (BFLA)
steps: Recover admin/privileged routes the low role never sees: JS bundles, mobile client, OpenAPI/Swagger, docs, route manifests.
Replay each privileged action with a low-privilege session (and with no session) — change only the auth, not the body.
Try method/verb tampering and header overrides (X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-Original-URL) on blocked paths.
Confirm the action actually executed server-side (state changed), not just a 200 on a no-op.
Prove the least-damaging privileged action; do not perform destructive admin operations.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model enumerate likely admin route names from the app's naming conventions in the recovered bundle.

methodologies.name: Mass assignment / over-posting
steps: GET the object and note every field the server returns (role, isAdmin, verified, balance, ownerId, emailVerified).
Add those fields to a PATCH/PUT/POST body that normally omits them.
Re-read the object to confirm the field persisted — a 200 is not proof, the stored value is.
Escalate: bind a role/owner/tenant field to take over or cross a boundary.
Report with the exact field, before/after values, and the privilege gained.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to diff the GET response schema against the accepted write body to propose over-postable fields.

methodologies.name: Cross-tenant escalation
steps: Find the client-supplied tenant selector: X-Org-Id, workspaceId, account_id, a subdomain slug, or a tenant claim in the JWT.
Create two tenants. From tenant A, set the selector to tenant B on an otherwise-authorized request.
Verify the server re-validates tenant ownership server-side, not just structurally.
Read one B record to prove the crossing; check write paths separately.
Document the selector, where it is trusted, and the blast radius across tenants.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: let the model map which endpoints echo the tenant selector unchanged vs re-derive it from the session.

methodologies.name: Full-read SSRF
steps: Find a parameter the server fetches (url=, webhook, import-by-URL, link preview, PDF/screenshot renderer).
Point it at an OOB collaborator to confirm the fetch happens and from which egress IP.
Point at 127.0.0.1 and common internal ports; diff response bodies and timings for open vs closed.
If the body returns, you have a proxy into the private network — enumerate minimally to prove reach.
Do NOT pivot further than one internal read needed to prove impact. Never touch third-party hosts.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to generate filter-bypass variants (decimal/octal/IPv6-mapped, redirect, DNS-rebind) for the specific validator observed.

methodologies.name: Cloud metadata access
steps: Confirm an SSRF primitive first (see Full-read / Blind SSRF).
Target 169.254.169.254 (AWS IMDSv1), metadata.google.internal (+ required header), and the Azure/Alibaba/Oracle equivalents; 169.254.170.2 for ECS task roles.
If IMDSv1 responds, retrieve the role name then the temporary credentials — capture only enough to prove validity.
Validate the credentials are live (e.g. sts get-caller-identity) WITHOUT touching customer data or making changes.
Report as cloud credential theft (P1) — this has stopped being a web bug. Redact the secret in the report.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model identify the cloud provider from response fingerprints and name the exact metadata paths to try.

methodologies.name: Blind SSRF
steps: Trigger the fetch and confirm via OOB DNS/HTTP callback that the server reached out.
Establish an open/closed port oracle via differential timing or redirect-depth encoding.
Attempt to convert to full-read via HTTP redirect loops or error-based leakage.
Chain toward IMDS or an internal service; blind-only is a lead, not a standalone report.
Note the manual conditions still needed (e.g. IMDSv1 reachable) before claiming impact.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to design a redirect-loop payload that encodes the internal response length.

methodologies.name: SQL injection
steps: Find a parameter reaching a query; a single quote that changes the response is the first tell.
Confirm with boolean (AND 1=1 vs AND 1=2) and time-based (SLEEP/pg_sleep/WAITFOR) differentials.
For UNION, find the column count via ORDER BY, then match types.
Extract ONLY a version string or current_user as proof — never dump tables or PII.
Check second-order: store a payload in one feature, trigger it where another reads it into a query.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model propose DB-specific payloads once the backend (MySQL/Postgres/MSSQL/Oracle) is fingerprinted.

methodologies.name: Server-Side Template Injection
steps: Inject a math expression into any reflected field: {{7*7}}, ${7*7}, <%= 7*7 %>, #{7*7}.
A rendered 49 identifies template evaluation; the exact polyglot that works identifies the engine.
Map engine → sandbox-escape primitive (Jinja2 config/__class__, Freemarker new, Velocity, ERB).
Prove RCE non-destructively (id / whoami equivalent) then STOP.
Test error-based/blind SSTI where a malformed expression leaks the value in an exception.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model for the minimal sandbox-escape chain for the confirmed engine and version.

methodologies.name: OS command injection
steps: Target features that shell out: file conversion, PDF/image handling, network tooling, backups.
Try separators and substitution: ; | & $(id) `id` %0a, plus argument injection (leading -).
Confirm blind execution via an OOB DNS/HTTP callback from the injected command.
Capture command output through the OOB channel or a response reflection; prove with id/hostname.
Verify non-destructively; never run commands that alter or exfiltrate data.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: let the model suggest argument-injection flags for the specific binary the feature invokes.

methodologies.name: Authentication bypass
steps: Map the auth flow end to end; look for any route to an authenticated state without valid credentials.
Test response manipulation (success:false→true), forced browsing past a step, and token-not-verified paths.
Check JWT handling: alg:none, RS256→HS256 confusion, weak secret, kid/jku injection.
Confirm you reach an authenticated action as a different user, not just a cosmetic logged-in state.
Use a throwaway/test account as the victim; never target real users.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to enumerate the state transitions in the captured flow and flag the unguarded one.

methodologies.name: OTP / 2FA brute force
steps: Request an OTP and inspect length, lifetime, and whether the attempt counter resets on resend.
Brute within the rate window; use GraphQL alias batching or parallel requests to beat per-request limits.
Check OTP-not-bound-to-user: request as yourself, submit against the victim's account.
Confirm a successful bypass reaches the protected action; stop at one proof.
Only ever brute your own test account's code.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model compute the expected attempts vs the observed limit to decide if brute is in scope.

methodologies.name: Predictable password reset token
steps: Request several reset tokens in quick succession for accounts you control.
Compare them byte-by-byte: look for timestamps, counters, md5(email), or low-entropy structure.
Check Host-header poisoning: does the reset link honor an attacker Host/X-Forwarded-Host?
Check token lifecycle: reuse after login, no invalidation on new request, long expiry.
Prove takeover against your own second test account; never a real user.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to estimate token entropy and propose the generation scheme from the samples.

methodologies.name: Weak redirect_uri validation
steps: Enumerate registered redirect_uris, then test loose matching: prefix/suffix/wildcard, added path, different port/scheme.
Try bypasses: https://target.com.evil.tld, /callback/../../, a # or ? truncation, open-redirect chain.
If the code/token lands on an attacker origin, you have the takeover primitive.
Confirm the leaked code is exchangeable (or the token usable) before claiming ATO.
Chain with an open redirect on the trusted origin when direct redirect_uri is strict.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: let the model generate redirect_uri mutation candidates tailored to the observed validation rule.

methodologies.name: Race condition on a limit (limit overrun)
steps: Find a check-then-act on a limited resource: coupon, withdrawal, invite, vote, balance.
Fire ~20 identical requests simultaneously (single-packet attack over HTTP/2) to collapse jitter.
Measure STATE after, not status codes: did the balance/count exceed the server-enforced limit?
Reproduce to rule out flukes; capture the over-limit end state as proof.
Use minimal value amounts; restore/limit any real-money side effects.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to identify which of the captured endpoints share the same non-atomic counter.

methodologies.name: Payment bypass
steps: Map the full payment flow: cart → confirmation → provider callback → fulfillment.
Test client-trusted status (mark paid client-side), unverified/forgeable provider callback, test-mode key in prod.
Tamper amount/currency between quote and capture; try $0, negative, and currency-swap.
Confirm the order reaches a fulfilled/paid state without real payment.
Use the smallest possible order and reverse any side effects.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: have the model check whether the provider callback signature/timestamp is actually verified in the captured traffic.

methodologies.name: Unrestricted upload to RCE
steps: Identify where uploads are stored and whether that path is server-executed.
Bypass filters: double extension (shell.php.jpg), magic-byte prefix, content-type spoof, .htaccess/web.config, multipart filename tricks.
Retrieve the uploaded file's URL and request it to trigger execution.
Prove execution with a benign marker (echo/id) — never a full webshell on a live target.
If direct execution is blocked, chain with LFI/path traversal to include the upload.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to rank bypass techniques by the server stack fingerprinted from headers/errors.

methodologies.name: Java deserialization
steps: Spot serialized input: ac ed 00 05 magic or rO0AB base64 in a cookie, parameter, or queue message.
Fingerprint libraries on the classpath (Commons-Collections, Spring, Groovy, Hibernate) via errors/behavior.
Build a gadget chain for a confirmed library; confirm blind execution via an OOB callback.
Prove RCE non-destructively (DNS callback from the deserialized gadget) then stop.
Never run destructive gadgets on a live target.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: let the model match the fingerprinted library versions to a known-working gadget chain.

methodologies.name: Prompt injection, indirect
steps: Find content the agent ingests on someone else's behalf: a page it fetches, a doc/ticket/email, a repo file, a calendar invite.
Plant instructions in that content (including hidden/zero-width/HTML-comment text) that redirect the agent's tool calls.
Target a real capability: exfiltrate via a tool, call an internal URL (SSRF), or perform an unauthorized action.
Confirm the agent acted on the injected instruction, not just echoed it.
Prove with a benign exfil marker to a collaborator; never exfiltrate real data.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: this class IS the AI surface — use a second model to generate injection phrasings that survive the app's guardrail.

methodologies.name: Dependency confusion
steps: Harvest internal package names from lockfiles, bundles, Dockerfiles, CI logs, and error messages.
Check whether each internal name is unclaimed on the public registry (npm/PyPI/etc.).
If claimable, register a benign higher-version placeholder that only beacons on install (no payload).
Confirm the build/CI pulled your package via the OOB beacon — that beacon IS the report.
Publish nothing malicious; report immediately and request takedown.
methodologies.ai_hook: Optional: ask the model to extract candidate internal package names from the recovered manifests and logs.
